messages.content:
Dear participants,

It is great to see how strong the community’s solvers have become. In response to requests for new test problems, we have prepared a stress-test dataset that mirrors the configuration of the final Stage 2 main leaderboard evaluation:

https://huggingface.co/datasets/SAIRfoundation/equational-theories-selected-problems/viewer/stage2_stress_test

The dataset contains 200 problems across four difficulty categories, with 50 problems in each category: 25 true and 25 false.

  • order4_normal
  • order4_hard
  • order4_extra_hard
  • order5_normal

Each problem is worth one point. The final Stage 2 main leaderboard evaluation will use the same category distribution and scoring setup. You can use this dataset to stress-test and finalize your solver before submission.

We are also preparing harder Order-5 problems for experimentation and research. These problems will be available as an additional community challenge and will not be included in the main leaderboard evaluation.

Thank you for your participation and support!
messages.subject: New Stage 2 Stress-Test Dataset

messages.content:
Thank you for the stress-test set!

I had asked for around 100 fresh equations to really test the robustness of our solver before submission, so getting 200 problems matching the final leaderboard distribution was an even better test than expected. :slight_smile:

Our current solver is a single self-contained Python file of about 406 KB. On the full 200-problem stress test, it reached:
200/200 solved - 0 failed
Total solver time: 741.2 s
Wall-clock time: 12m25.6s

This was across all four categories, including the Order-5 problems, with Lean-accepted certificates.

What was especially satisfying is that it also solved the two particularly stubborn Order-5 residuals we had been working on. Those were the cases that forced us to improve the proof-search architecture rather than simply add more brute force.

At this point, my main remaining uncertainty is simply whether everything behaves exactly the same in the official evaluation environment. Fingers crossed. :slight_smile:

One small question about the final leaderboard: in the event of a tie on the number of correctly solved problems, is there any secondary criterion such as total solving time or submission size, or is the ranking based strictly on the number of solved problems? Just curious about how ties are handled.

Thank you again for providing such a useful benchmark.

Now that “hard” and “extra hard” are behaving rather nicely… any chance of an ULTRA HARD experimental category? :wink:
Purely for science, of course.

Good luck to everyone for the final submissions!

messages.content:
@Wenlin Zhang

Thanks, and thank you for sharing your results too!

After the 200-problem stress test, I also ran one final full regression over our combined Stage 2 validation set: 2,130 problems aggregated across the available benchmark categories, all with the exact same solver version.

Result:
2130/2130 solved — 0 failed
Total solver time: 7170.1 s
Wall-clock: 119m56.7s
about 3.37 s/problem on average.

Most importantly for me, the entire run was fully deterministic, zero LLM calls.

So the same single-file solver now passes both the 200-problem stress test and this much larger 2,130-problem regression set without a failure.

Under the hood it has become a fairly hardcore mix of equational rewriting, guided superposition, finite countermodel construction and Lean certificate generation... although I suspect that part may impress the solver more than the leaderboard. :smile:

At this point I think I’ve tested it about as hard as I reasonably can before submission.

See you on the final leaderboard!

messages.content:
@Axabra 2130/2130 fully deterministic is a great way to go into the deadline — congrats, and see you on the leaderboard!

I had similar experiences, fully deterministic is possible, LLM is not needed. But in a certain way I had the hope for an LLM as a white knight, but Determinism is much stronger for equational theory .

On a different note: now that the deadline has passed, I've pulled the algorithms out of my solver into a small open-source library, mostly so the work doesn't die with the competition — eqtheory (pip install eqtheory, https://github.com/osick/eqtheory , MIT Licence). E-graphs with proof extraction, superposition, finite/infinite countermodel search, and Lean 4 certificates that are now self-contained (plain toolchain, no Mathlib, no judge repo). It solves the 200-problem stress set and some more, but it's a young codebase with obvious gaps: it only knows one binary operation, the term parser is rigid, the Fin > 12 search could really use a proper SAT backend and more. If any of that overlaps with what you built for Stage 2 — or you just want to run your stress numbers against it — issues and PRs are very welcome. I'd honestly rather merge a better model finder than write one.

And if someone wants to prototype the ULTRA HARD category: the ETP's Austin pairs (true in every finite magma, false anyway) are sitting right there. :mushroom:

messages.content:
Congratulations on the deterministic run @Oliver Sick and thanks for putting eqtheory out rather than letting the work die with the competition. We landed in the same place independently: our solver settles everything deterministically with zero LLM calls; the fallback exists and never fired once. Three or four of us converging on "determinism beats the LLM here" is starting to look like a fact about the problem rather than a preference.

Ours is public now, in case any of it is useful to you: https://github.com/the-omega-institute/sair-eqt2-stage2-solver — single file, stdlib only, with the run ledgers and a write-up at arXiv:2609.00706.

Two things that speak directly to the gaps you named:

The Fin > 12 wall. We stopped feeding large carriers through a finOpTable at all. Above n = 10 the certificate emits the operation as arithmetic inside a submission.op namespace, so the kernel never has to chew a table — and as a side effect those certificates close over no axioms at all, while the decide-on-table ones pull in the usual three. That may be a cheaper answer than a SAT backend for a good part of the range.

Before the model finder runs at all, we try structured families — linear and affine magmas mod n (n <= 50), F_p^k vector-linear, polynomial — where finding a countermodel is solving for coefficients rather than searching a space. The Latin-square-propagating search over carriers 4-10 only sees what those miss. Splitting the work that way is most of why the search never became the bottleneck.

Also, a robustness note for the rigid parser, since it nearly cost us everything: some official problem files use * for the operation while the repository and playground use the diamond. We normalize both at every intake. An unpatched solver scores zero on a *-encoded file, silently.

Happy to keep talking, issues or here, either way.
